analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from buying individual stocks and requires public notice before sales.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 15 Republican cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Homeland Security committee with no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying individual stocks or stock derivatives like options. Before any sale of a stock they still hold, the member would have to publicly announce it 7 to 14 days in advance, so the public can see it coming. Violators would owe a fee of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade's value, plus any profit made, and could not pay that fee out of official office accounts or campaign donations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know their lawmakers aren't trading on nonpublic information they learn in office. Members who follow the rules also gain a clearer defense against suspicion, because every sale is announced in advance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters worried about congressional insider trading

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children could no longer buy individual stocks, options, or similar instruments that bet on a specific company's price.
Every sale would require a public notice filed 7 to 14 days ahead, posted online by the House Clerk or Senate Secretary, including the date, description, and number of shares.
Violations carry a fee equal to the greater of $2,000 or 10% of the trade's value, plus any net gain realized, and members could not pay it from their official expense accounts or campaign funds.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their immediate families, who would give up the ability to buy individual stocks and would have to pre-announce every sale. They can still hold diversified mutual funds, small-business stakes, and blind trusts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The bill bans new purchases but does not require members to sell stocks they already own, so a member could keep large positions in companies their committees oversee for years.

The exceptions are broad: trades by a spouse or child made through their job or as part of professional duties are exempt, and trusts are allowed as long as the member cannot direct them and the trustee is not a family member.

Enforcement is mostly financial: the penalty is a fee paid to the Treasury, and a referral to the Attorney General is only available if the member resigns or retires before paying, so an sitting member who violates the rule faces no criminal process under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rules are real and enforceable: no new individual-stock purchases, advance public notice of sales, and a fee that claws back profits. But an honest supporter would acknowledge the gaps — existing holdings can be kept indefinitely, job-related trades by family members are exempt, and there is no requirement to fully divest, which other proposals have included. As written, it closes the most visible abuses while leaving members substantial room to stay invested in the market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Pete Ricketts introduced the bill on March 18, 2026, joined by six original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which is the only action it has received.
Fifteen Republican senators have cosponsored it; no Democrat has joined, and no vote has taken place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, members of Congress are better off: the bill has not moved, so they retain the ability to buy and sell individual stocks, subject only to the current disclosure rules. The outcome is not final, since the session runs to January 2027.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who can still trade stocks, for now

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans and no Democrat has signed on, but with no hearing or vote yet, partisan opposition has not been demonstrated — the bill has simply not moved in committee.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their immediate families
industries.note: They would lose the ability to buy individual stocks and would have to announce every sale 7 to 14 days before making it, with fees of at least 10% of the trade plus any gains for violations. Their interest in keeping quiet, unrestricted trading runs against the public's interest in seeing lawmakers' trades before they happen.

analysis.trajectory: Stock-trading ban bills have repeatedly stalled in committee in past Congresses, and this one has drawn no committee action in its first months despite 16 Republican sponsors. It is unlikely to reach the floor unless Senate leadership schedules it, and the absence of any Democratic cosponsor makes broad bipartisan action unlikely before the session ends in January 2027.
